analysis.investment_thesis: Delhivery reported its first annual net profit of a mere INR 162 Cr in FY25 after six consecutive years of losses totalling thousands of crores — it has no established earning power in any sense Graham recognises. A P/E of 192x and P/B of 3.6x on a company that just crossed breakeven is the very definition of speculation dressed as investment.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 32.5% over six years reflects genuine market share gains in Indian e-commerce logistics
Debt/equity of only 0.17 — the balance sheet is not dangerously leveraged
OCF turned consistently positive in FY24–25, suggesting the unit economics are improving directionally
key_risks: Six years of net losses totalling well over INR 4,700 Cr — the business has destroyed capital on a massive scale; one profitable year does not constitute a track record
At a P/E of 192x and forward P/E of 55x, the stock discounts an enormous earnings ramp that has not yet materialized and may never achieve adequate returns on the capital deployed
Operating margin of 0.79% offers no cushion; a modest volume decline or competitive pricing action could return the company to losses immediately
red_flags: No promoter holding — the founding team appears to have largely exited; shareholders are almost entirely institutional, with no skin-in-the-game owner-operator to create long-term value discipline
Other income of INR 442 Cr in FY25 nearly matches operating income of INR 376 Cr — the company's 'profit' is heavily dependent on investment income, not core logistics operations
EV/EBITDA of −767.8x (negative) and five-year accumulated losses disqualify this stock from every quantitative filter in Graham's framework; this is an IPO-era growth story, not a value investment
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Delhivery is a venture-capital-backed logistics roll-up that went public in 2022 at a premium only an investment bank could love. From Graham's vantage point, the analysis is mercifully brief: a company must demonstrate consistent earning power before it deserves any valuation premium, and Delhivery has demonstrated the opposite — sustained, large losses for most of its public life. The FY25 profit of INR 162 Cr on INR 8,932 Cr revenue implies a net margin of 1.8%, and that figure is flattered by INR 442 Cr of other (investment) income.

The logistics sector in India is structurally competitive and capital-intensive; Delhivery faces Zomato-backed Shiprocket, Blue Dart, and Ecom Express. Durable pricing power is unproven. Even if management succeeds in scaling margins, the current market capitalisation of INR 34,676 Cr prices in perfection over many years of execution. Graham's counsel is clear: when the seller (institutional investors and the IPO) knows more than the buyer, the buyer's only protection is price — and at these levels, there is none.
